extracted.intended_audience: health services researchers, hospital leaders/administrators, and clinicians interested in physician engagement and organizational culture
extracted.subtask_description: A qualitative mixed-methods investigation of professional cultural dynamics between physicians and administrators at an academic medical center, and how those dynamics affect physician engagement, including design, analysis, findings, and institution-specific interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of physician engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Physician engagement is loosely defined as 'the degree to which physicians feel fulfilled and satisfied by their work, supported within their organization, and motivated to continue their work, recommend their organization, and be involved within their organization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this multidimensional definition when selecting outcomes or interpreting engagement measures; engagement links to productivity, fewer medical mistakes, and lower turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of standard engagement surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard measures (e.g., National Health Service’s Medical Engagement Scale, proprietary tools like Press Ganey) 'are well-equipped to indicate whether an issue exists but not necessarily why physicians do not feel engaged or how best to support them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat surveys as diagnostic for existence of problems but supplement with sensitive qualitative methods to understand underlying causes and inform targeted interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of HuNamic analysis (customized mixed-methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: HuNamic analysis entails an efficient, customized mixed methods analysis based on the qualitative question(s) of interest: researchers design a customized approach with subjects and use multiple qualitative methods together in tandem via an iterative process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: arrives at thematic saturation and core themes more efficiently. Disadvantage: 'prohibits review and discussion of the final results of the separate methodologies.' Use when rapid, integrated insights are prioritized, but be explicit about methodological trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful sampling across roles and specialties
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruitment was purposeful: 20 physicians across specialties and 20 healthcare administrators across management levels, with cohorts balanced for gender and broad experience (1–35 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying organizational culture, purposefully recruit across relevant roles and experience ranges to capture heterogeneity; report participation rates (here 77% physicians, 83% administrators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation rate and sample-size transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Report participation rates and sample composition (e.g., 20/26 physicians participated; cohorts of equal men and women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reported participation rates to assess representativeness and possible selection bias; justify sample size with thematic saturation evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Study reviewed by IRB and deemed exempt; informed verbal consent obtained and documented. Authors agreed to maintain anonymity of institution and participants; data cannot be made publicly available due to ethical and legal restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When topics are sensitive and could jeopardize careers, implement strong anonymity protections, get IRB review, and clearly document data-sharing limitations and procedures for data access requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection methods: semi-structured interviews and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semi-structured interviews and observations; interviews begin with rapport-building and progress to more sensitive questions using prompts like 'why do you think that?' and 'what do you think drives that?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine interviews with observation and field notes to capture both reported and observed behaviors; provide interview script (S1 Table) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbatim transcription and use of field notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed alongside field notes from observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim transcripts plus field notes support thorough qualitative analysis and cross-method triangulation; state transcription methods and tools used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative inductive–deductive analytic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Data collection and analysis occurred simultaneously using an iterative inductive-deductive approach; grounded theory, phenomenology, and discourse analysis were performed in tandem on transcripts with field notes guiding additional data collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterative analysis allows early codes to inform subsequent data collection; document how inductive and deductive cycles were balanced and how methods informed each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation of qualitative methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied constructivist grounded theory, phenomenology, and discourse analysis together to understand social structure, internalized conceptualizations, and expressed behavior respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple analytic lenses to capture different facets of cultural dynamics; describe how findings from each method were integrated and any tensions between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of qualitative analysis software
rubrics_metrics.description: NVivo 11.0 was used for data management and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State software and versions used to facilitate reproducibility; describe coding procedures and provide final coding structure when possible (S2 Table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic saturation reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Thematic saturation occurred after approximately 10 interviews per cohort, but all 40 participants were interviewed given heterogeneity and use of novel analytic approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how saturation was assessed and justify continued sampling decisions when heterogeneity or method warrants additional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-analyst consistency vs. bias
rubrics_metrics.description: All interviews and analyses were performed by a single researcher which 'ensured a consistent approach' but 'exposed the analysis to considerable bias.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge trade-offs of single-analyst designs; mitigate bias via stakeholder validation, auditing, or multiple coders where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder validation and feedback as part of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary themes were presented and discussed with ≈400 physicians and administrators to provide critical feedback regarding validity and helpfulness; these presentations also functioned as interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large-group feedback sessions to validate findings, refine interpretations, and increase utility; document how feedback altered interpretations or interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about funding and competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare funding sources and competing interests (e.g., authors' involvement in HuNamics, LLC) and whether these affected the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full disclosure is required; explain how potential conflicts were managed and whether external funders influenced analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and external validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge limitations: single institution, modest sample size relative to entire organization, single analyzer who had prior clinician training potentially biasing characterization, cross-sectional design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state limitations and caution against overgeneralization; recommend multi-institutional comparisons for broader generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed cultural differences as analytic dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Key analytic dimensions included professional background/values (physicians: individual success, specialty identity; administrators: team/organization focus) and decision-making styles (physicians: short V-shaped, administrators: longer W-shaped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying interprofessional relations, code for identity, socialization, time-horizon/acuity, and decision-making styles; use schematics (Fig 1, Fig 2) to represent social processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of perceived organizational issues to assess
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived problems included centralized scheduling, work relative value unit (wRVU)–based compensation, reduction of support staff, lack of transparency, ineffective meetings, and lack of effective physician leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete organizational changes and policies as focal prompts in interviews to elicit how policy affects culture and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of common solutions' conflicting connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although participants commonly proposed similar solutions (increase transparency/communication, align incentives, spend more time in each other’s worlds), language analysis revealed conflicting connotations (orientations as 'bosses/islands' vs 'partners/leaders') that can undermine efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing interventions, analyze the underlying connotations and power dynamics; ensure shared language and meanings to avoid reinforcing hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical interventions and implementation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions described and/or implemented included presentations/discussions of results to stakeholders, bimonthly unstructured meetings between physician groups and trusted clinician-administrators, physician leadership training programs, avoiding the word 'manage,' tailoring conversations by specialty, and using physical presence to establish rapport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions should be context-specific, validated with stakeholders, and designed to shift connotations toward partnership; combine awareness-raising with leadership development and structured opportunities for cross-world presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of leadership and leadership development
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective leadership is central: leaders should empower others, facilitate integration, and support physician leaders or partners; creating physician leadership programs and clear expectations helps engender effective physician leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in leadership development and role clarity; align leadership selection/training with desired integrative behaviors rather than purely managerial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys alone are insufficient—use qualitative analyses to design targeted tools
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'difficult if not impossible to understand the cultural complexities of professional groups within an organization with surveys alone,' therefore qualitative analyses are needed to design targeted interventions and organization-specific surveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative findings to tailor survey items and interpret survey results in local language and context; combine methodologies for diagnostic and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data access procedures when data cannot be publicly shared
rubrics_metrics.description: When data cannot be publicly released due to ethical/legal constraints, provide clear instructions for requests (e.g., IRB contact, corresponding author) and reference study/IRB numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document data-sharing limitations and established process for case-by-case access; include IRB contact and reference numbers to facilitate legitimate requests.
